info.bio:
Ted Nugent (1948) es un guitarrista estadounidense que se mueve entre el rock clásico, el hard rock y el heavy metal.

Su canción de más éxito probablemente haya sido "cat scratch fever", sus directos siempre han sido poderosos y dinámicos.

Theodore "Ted Nugent" (13 de diciembre de 1948) es un guitarrista de Hard rock originario de Detroit, Michigan. Originalmente saltó a la fama como el líder de Amboy Dukes.

Su estilo es esencialmente rockero

scenes.name: Psicodelia y acid rock
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: La segunda fuente del heavy, que se suma a la estructura del blues rock: letras misteriosas de viaje de ácido, ropa de colores y espectáculos de luces (el heavy conservará los light shows de 1967). Musicalmente es como el jazz pero con repetición de frases simples; no apunta a las piernas sino a la cabeza, y perderse en la música es «entenderla», un uso extático que el heavy retoma en clave dionisíaca. Muchos pioneros del heavy empezaron aquí: Judas Priest con Rocka Rolla, Lemmy en Hawkwind, Ted Nugent en los Amboy Dukes, Uriah Heep a caballo entre ambos, y Pink Floyd, cuyos discos conceptuales de finales de los setenta se acercan al heavy.

scenes.name: La radio: del exilio a Z-Rock
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Durante su primera década el heavy casi no suena en la radio: la FM progresiva rechaza a Black Sabbath por cambiar «love» por «evil», el AOR de los consultores solo pone «Stairway to Heaven» y algo de AC/DC, y a los anunciantes no les interesan los chicos de quince a dieciocho años. Weinstein ve ventajas en ese exilio: obliga a las bandas a girar sin parar (Aerosmith, Blue Öyster Cult y Ted Nugent, más de cuarenta semanas al año), las une a su público, las libra de los códigos radiofónicos (canciones de ocho minutos como «War Pigs», solos largos, el disco y no el single como unidad) y explica la abundancia de discos en directo. En los ochenta llegan los programas de metal en las radios universitarias (WSOU de Seton Hall se pasa entera al metal), el informe metal de CMJ y su Metal Marathon, y en la radio comercial el formato por satélite Z-Rock desde Dallas, que relega el thrash a su «Headbanger’s Heaven» nocturno. En Gran Bretaña, el único refugio es el «Friday Night Rock Show» de la BBC con Tommy Vance. Cuando la radio comercial acepta el metal es a través de MTV y de las power ballads, y exige productores de éxitos y solos recortados; aun así Metallica vende un millón de …And Justice for All sin apenas sonar.

podcast.title: Rolling Stone Cover (March 9, 1979)
podcast.body: Ted Nugent was featured on the cover of Rolling Stone magazine on March 9, 1979, signifying his significant presence and popularity in the music scene during that period. "So I happen to have in my hands a copy of Rolling Stone magazine dated March 9, 1979 and there is Ted Nugent on the cover."

podcast.title: Attempt to Purchase Muzak for Closure
podcast.body: Guitarist Ted Nugent notoriously offered $10 million to acquire the Muzak company, with his stated intention being to shut it down entirely. This act underscored his profound disdain for the genre and its widespread presence. "Según sus palabras, Muzak era... Más provecho sacobra y aninó la propuesta del Muzak."

podcast.title: Audience Demands
podcast.body: Nugent was known for explicitly demanding an intense reaction from his concert audiences, stating that if they weren't "foaming at the mouth after 40 minutes," he felt he hadn't performed his job adequately. This aggressive performance style occasionally led to fights and arrests among attendees. "he said that he literally demanded a reaction from them in his shows. And if they weren't foaming at the mouth after 40 minutes and he had not done his job."

podcast.title: Banning of Outdoor Concerts in Charlotte
podcast.body: Following an outdoor concert by Ted Nugent and his band at the Memorial Colosseum in Charlotte, North Carolina, the city council banned all future outdoor concerts, perceiving Nugent and rock music as a menace to society. "Nugent was loud to the point that after he and his band played an outdoor concert at the Memorial Colosseum in Charlotte, North Carolina, the city council banned outdoor concerts."

podcast.title: Defense Against "Noise" Criticism
podcast.body: In a 1977 newspaper article, Ted Nugent defended his music against critics who dismissed it as "simply noise." He argued that he would be a "pretty bad musician after all these years if he'd only learned three chords and how to make noise with them," citing "Stranglehold" as an example of a melodically and influentially rich composition. "However, Nugent also defended his music and said that he would be a pretty bad musician after all these years if he'd only learned three chords and how to make noise with them."

podcast.title: Defiance of Music Industry
podcast.body: Nugent's early solo career faced considerable resistance from the music industry, with "every record label passed" on him. They found his feedback-laden, guitar-jamming style and song themes, like "Stranglehold," unappealing. Despite this, his success, fueled by dedicated fans and unparalleled concert energy, served as a direct challenge to the industry's initial rejection. "The music industry passed every record label passed on Ted Nugent. He's got that feedback entitled. It's all a guitar jamming type stuff and he sings songs about Strangleholds. Now we'll pass, everybody passed."

podcast.title: Embodiment of Rock for Some Critics
podcast.body: Patrick Yack, writing for the Florida Times Union in Jacksonville a year after Nugent's impactful performances, observed that "too many Ted Nugent is rock," underscoring his strong association with the genre's essence. "Patrick Yack, who was writing for the Florida Times Union in Jacksonville a year later said that too many Ted Nugent is rock."

podcast.title: Energetic and Provocative Live Performances
podcast.body: Ted Nugent was known for his loud, high-energy stage presence, screaming into the microphone, leaping around, and using profanity, which contributed to his reputation as a feared rock and roll figure by parents. He also fabricated stories about hunting and consuming wild animals raw. "He screamed into the microphone. He leapt around the stage dropping F-bums. He made up stories about hunting wild animals and eating them raw."

podcast.title: Fan Demographics
podcast.body: Ted Nugent's description of his fans included "guys out there in pick up trucks who talk four-wheel drive with me," "guys out there with amplifiers and guitars who talk music with me," and "guys out there with big grins on their faces who talk pussy with me." He also observed that "a couple thousand out of 20,000" at his shows were "wound it," suggesting a diverse audience seeking various forms of engagement, from shared hobbies to intense emotional release. "Nugent said, I think most of them have a basic knowledge and grip and focus of their talents."

podcast.title: Negative Media Portrayal in Charlotte News
podcast.body: The July 15, 1978, edition of the Charlotte News dedicated an entire page to Ted Nugent, depicting him and, by extension, rock music as a societal menace to the citizens of Charlotte. "An entire page of the July 15, 1978 edition of the Charlotte news was dedicated to Nugent and what a menace to society he and therefore rock music was to the fine citizens of Charlotte."

podcast.title: Stance on Music's Influence
podcast.body: Ted Nugent believed that if his music instigated violence or brought out negative behavior in a listener, it was because the individual was already "screwed up." "Nugent's view on it was that if listening to his music somehow brought out the worst in a kid, it led them to violence or something, then they were already screwed up."

podcast.title: Supported Donald Trump
podcast.body: Ted Nugent was one of the musicians who publicly supported Donald Trump, distinguishing himself from many artists who refused to perform at Trump's events. "Outside of Kid Rock, Ted Nugent, three doors down and ace freely."

xref.title: Early Professional Gigs and "Osterizer" (1968)
xref.body: The band's first professional gig was opening for the Amboy Dukes (featuring Ted Nugent) on January 20, 1968, followed by an opening slot for Blood Sweat and Tears on March 3, 1968. During these shows, Iggy notably played a homemade instrument called the "Osterizer," which was a vacuum cleaner attached to a blender, although he soon abandoned it due to amplification difficulties. "And was the singer playing a vacuum cleaner? Yes, yes it was. And was it attached to a blender? And yeah, it was."
